{{field-1}}"] ["question-99bfd564-d6cc-54a4-9108-196e20d54d83" :question/worked-solution "We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}) & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{2}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=6\sqrt{x} & \,⟹\,v=\int 6\sqrt{x}\,dx=4{x}^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}6\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{e}u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})(4{x}^{3/2}){|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}(4{x}^{3/2})(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[4{e}^{3/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-4(1)^{3/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡((1)^{2})]-8{\int }_{1}^{e}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{e}^{3/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-\frac{16{x}^{3/2}}{3}{|}_{1}^{{e}^{4}} \\  & =8{e}^{3/2}-(\frac{16{e}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(24{e}^{3/2}-16{e}^{3/2}+16) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(8{e}^{3/2}+16) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}({e}^{3/2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-99bfd564-d6cc-54a4-9108-196e20d54d83" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-685af73e-aa69-5aab-a314-fb7262dca792" :answer-field/id #uuid "685af73e-aa69-5aab-a314-fb7262dca792"] ["answer-d9beb126-d816-586d-81d2-7d8e3cd3f21e" :answer/id #uuid "d9beb126-d816-586d-81d2-7d8e3cd3f21e"] ["answer-d9beb126-d816-586d-81d2-7d8e3cd3f21e" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d9beb126-d816-586d-81d2-7d8e3cd3f21e" :answer/value "\frac{8e^{3/2}+16}{3}"] ["answer-field-685af73e-aa69-5aab-a314-fb7262dca792" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-685af73e-aa69-5aab-a314-fb7262dca792" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-685af73e-aa69-5aab-a314-fb7262dca792" :answer-field/correct "answer-d9beb126-d816-586d-81d2-7d8e3cd3f21e"] ["answer-field-685af73e-aa69-5aab-a314-fb7262dca792" :answer-field/choices "answer-d9beb126-d816-586d-81d2-7d8e3cd3f21e"] ["question-99bfd564-d6cc-54a4-9108-196e20d54d83" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-685af73e-aa69-5aab-a314-fb7262dca792"] [17592186096834 :knowledge-point/questions "question-99bfd564-d6cc-54a4-9108-196e20d54d83"] ["question-11666770-4f2b-5054-898a-6ed32728d68e" :question/id #uuid "11666770-4f2b-5054-898a-6ed32728d68e"] ["question-11666770-4f2b-5054-898a-6ed32728d68e" :question/math-academy-id "q-350955"] ["question-11666770-4f2b-5054-898a-6ed32728d68e" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}"] ["question-11666770-4f2b-5054-898a-6ed32728d68e" :question/worked-solution "We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=2{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int 2{x}^{2}\,dx=\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}\end{aligned}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}){|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\frac{2({e}^{2})^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2(1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)}{3}]-\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{6}}{3}-(\frac{2{e}^{6}}{9}-\frac{2}{9}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(12{e}^{6}-2{e}^{6}+2) \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(5{e}^{6}+1).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-11666770-4f2b-5054-898a-6ed32728d68e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a1b142ab-d4d9-5382-9f40-a044ab401784" :answer-field/id #uuid "a1b142ab-d4d9-5382-9f40-a044ab401784"] ["answer-4677848a-3850-5a75-8b53-cf4eed86d4b9" :answer/id #uuid "4677848a-3850-5a75-8b53-cf4eed86d4b9"] ["answer-4677848a-3850-5a75-8b53-cf4eed86d4b9" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-4677848a-3850-5a75-8b53-cf4eed86d4b9" :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}(5{e}^{6}+1)"] ["answer-field-a1b142ab-d4d9-5382-9f40-a044ab401784" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-a1b142ab-d4d9-5382-9f40-a044ab401784" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-a1b142ab-d4d9-5382-9f40-a044ab401784" :answer-field/correct "answer-4677848a-3850-5a75-8b53-cf4eed86d4b9"] ["answer-field-a1b142ab-d4d9-5382-9f40-a044ab401784" :answer-field/choices "answer-4677848a-3850-5a75-8b53-cf4eed86d4b9"] ["question-11666770-4f2b-5054-898a-6ed32728d68e" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-a1b142ab-d4d9-5382-9f40-a044ab401784"] [17592186096834 :knowledge-point/questions "question-11666770-4f2b-5054-898a-6ed32728d68e"] ["question-3c9f18f7-85c5-5539-81bc-9088568cf461" :question/id #uuid "3c9f18f7-85c5-5539-81bc-9088568cf461"] ["question-3c9f18f7-85c5-5539-81bc-9088568cf461" :question/math-academy-id "q-350948"] ["question-3c9f18f7-85c5-5539-81bc-9088568cf461" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. $$
\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x+1} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \,\text{d}x=x\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\,{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\cdot x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{x}{x+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use a substitution $x+1=u,$ thus $x=u-1$ and $\text{d}x=\text{d}u.$ Hence,

$$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-dec6c4d2-4bd8-5abe-a87c-7b60b0c36fa7" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}x(\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{log}_{5}⁡(({e}^{3})^{3})\,({e}^{3})-{log}_{5}⁡({1}^{3})\,(1)]-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3}{log}_{5}⁡({e}^{9})-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & ={e}^{3}\cdot \frac{9}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}({e}^{3}-1) \\  & =\frac{6{e}^{3}+3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dec6c4d2-4bd8-5abe-a87c-7b60b0c36fa7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-f39b1857-9db3-543c-8023-433cabfb635c" :answer-field/id #uuid "f39b1857-9db3-543c-8023-433cabfb635c"] ["answer-f35f40f9-7147-561f-97bb-d22e896e1a37" :answer/id #uuid "f35f40f9-7147-561f-97bb-d22e896e1a37"] ["answer-f35f40f9-7147-561f-97bb-d22e896e1a37" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-f35f40f9-7147-561f-97bb-d22e896e1a37" :answer/value "\frac{6{e}^{3}+3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}"] ["answer-field-f39b1857-9db3-543c-8023-433cabfb635c" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-f39b1857-9db3-543c-8023-433cabfb635c" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-f39b1857-9db3-543c-8023-433cabfb635c" :answer-field/correct "answer-f35f40f9-7147-561f-97bb-d22e896e1a37"] ["answer-field-f39b1857-9db3-543c-8023-433cabfb635c" :answer-field/choices "answer-f35f40f9-7147-561f-97bb-d22e896e1a37"] ["question-dec6c4d2-4bd8-5abe-a87c-7b60b0c36fa7" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-f39b1857-9db3-543c-8023-433cabfb635c"] [17592186096836 :knowledge-point/questions "question-dec6c4d2-4bd8-5abe-a87c-7b60b0c36fa7"] ["question-2827cc9e-45ac-55e8-ad01-41ef4d905442" :question/id #uuid "2827cc9e-45ac-55e8-ad01-41ef4d905442"] ["question-2827cc9e-45ac-55e8-ad01-41ef4d905442" :question/math-academy-id "q-351024"] ["question-2827cc9e-45ac-55e8-ad01-41ef4d905442" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}"] ["question-2827cc9e-45ac-55e8-ad01-41ef4d905442" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{2}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}x(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(({e}^{3})^{2})\,({e}^{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2})\,(1)]-2{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{6})-2x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & =6{e}^{3}-2({e}^{3}-1) \\  & =4{e}^{3}+2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2827cc9e-45ac-55e8-ad01-41ef4d905442" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-4c3f171c-fb81-5430-a177-4c369d89dfea" :answer-field/id #uuid "4c3f171c-fb81-5430-a177-4c369d89dfea"] ["answer-28f9591e-b52d-53c1-ad17-f0e9c703f814" :answer/id #uuid "28f9591e-b52d-53c1-ad17-f0e9c703f814"] ["answer-28f9591e-b52d-53c1-ad17-f0e9c703f814" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-28f9591e-b52d-53c1-ad17-f0e9c703f814" :answer/value "4e^3+2"] ["answer-field-4c3f171c-fb81-5430-a177-4c369d89dfea" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-4c3f171c-fb81-5430-a177-4c369d89dfea" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-4c3f171c-fb81-5430-a177-4c369d89dfea" :answer-field/correct "answer-28f9591e-b52d-53c1-ad17-f0e9c703f814"] ["answer-field-4c3f171c-fb81-5430-a177-4c369d89dfea" :answer-field/choices "answer-28f9591e-b52d-53c1-ad17-f0e9c703f814"] ["question-2827cc9e-45ac-55e8-ad01-41ef4d905442" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-4c3f171c-fb81-5430-a177-4c369d89dfea"] [17592186096836 :knowledge-point/questions "question-2827cc9e-45ac-55e8-ad01-41ef4d905442"] [17592186351405 :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/f2/f26c3e1bbbc268308db8d419bc799ad5349673e97c8828471997a5d36cb94d7d.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,(x-1)^{2}\le y\le x+1\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,(x-1)^{2}\le y\le 3-x\}.
$$

 

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2y\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2y\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{(x-1)^{2}}^{x+1}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{(x-1)^{2}}^{3-x}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}{|}_{(x-1)^{2}}^{x+1}\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}{|}_{(x-1)^{2}}^{3-x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(x+1)^{2}-(x-1)^{4}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}[(3-x)^{2}-(x-1)^{4}]\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(x-1)^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1}+{[-\frac{(3-x)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(x-1)^{5}}{5}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =((\frac{8}{3}-0)-(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{5}))+((-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5})-(-\frac{8}{3}-0)) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}+\frac{32}{15} \\  & =\frac{64}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5f7eccff-14bb-598f-9945-41d3d8682a45" :question/id #uuid "5f7eccff-14bb-598f-9945-41d3d8682a45"] ["question-5f7eccff-14bb-598f-9945-41d3d8682a45" :question/math-academy-id "q-82359"] ["question-5f7eccff-14bb-598f-9945-41d3d8682a45" :question/problem "Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=2x,$ $y=5-3x$ and $x=0.$
Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions."] ["question-5f7eccff-14bb-598f-9945-41d3d8682a45" :question/worked-solution "First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y=5-3x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{5-y}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$2x^2 - 27=5.$"] [17592186068475 :question/worked-solution "First, we isolate the $x^2$ on one side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-27 & =5 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =32 \\ {x}^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take the square root of both sides of the equation and solve the resulting absolute value equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{16} \\ |x| & =4 \\ x & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186068476 :question/problem "Solve for $p$ where $4p^2 - 11 = 14.$"] [17592186068476 :question/worked-solution "First, we isolate the $p^2$ on one side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{p}^{2}-11 & =14 \\ 4{p}^{2} & =25 \\ {p}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take the square root of both sides of the equation and solve the resulting absolute value equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{p}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |p| & =\frac{\sqrt{25}}{\sqrt{4}} \\ |p| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ p & =\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186068477 :question/problem "Find $t$ if $2t^2 = 36.$"] [17592186068477 :question/worked-solution "First, we isolate the $t^2$ on one side of the equation:

$$
\eqalign{
		2t^2 &= 36\
		t^2 &= 18
	}
$$

Then, we take the square root of both sides of the equation and solve the resulting absolute value equation:

$$
\eqalign{		
		\sqrt{t^2} &= \sqrt{18} \
		\vert t \vert &= \sqrt{18} \
		\vert t \vert &= \sqrt{9 \cdot 2} \
		\vert t \vert &= \sqrt{9} \cdot \sqrt{2} \
		\vert t \vert &= 3\sqrt{2} \
		t &= \pm 3\sqrt{2}
	}
$$"] ["question-f380333b-76ae-58b4-8fc8-adf9bbb2d3ab" :question/id #uuid "f380333b-76ae-58b4-8fc8-adf9bbb2d3ab"] ["question-f380333b-76ae-58b4-8fc8-adf9bbb2d3ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-44121"] ["question-f380333b-76ae-58b4-8fc8-adf9bbb2d3ab" :question/problem "Solve  $\frac{{q}^{2}}{2}-18=0.$"] ["question-f380333b-76ae-58b4-8fc8-adf9bbb2d3ab" :question/worked-solution "First, we isolate the ${q}^{2}$ on one side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{q}^{2}}{2}-18 & =0 \\ \frac{{q}^{2}}{2} & =18 \\ {q}^{2} & =2\cdot 18 \\ {q}^{2} & =36\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take the square root of both sides of the equation and solve the resulting absolute value equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{q}^{2}} & =\sqrt{36} \\ |q| & =6 \\ q & =\pm 6\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f380333b-76ae-58b4-8fc8-adf9bbb2d3ab" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-b72aded4-db5f-5673-ac54-684079de3588" :answer-field/id #uuid contains an $x^2$ term and a constant, it can be solved using the **square root method**. The square root method makes use of the fact that

$$
\sqrt{x^2} = \vert x \vert \,.
$$

To illustrate, we can solve the equation $2x^2-18=0$ using the following three steps:

1\. Isolate the $x^2$ on one side of the equation:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-18 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =18 \\ {x}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Take the square root of both sides of the equation

  $$
  \begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{9} \\ |x| & =3\end{aligned}
  $$

["question-60981b2b-035b-5158-a36c-3b0a5f268ae1" :question/math-academy-id "q-253560"] ["question-60981b2b-035b-5158-a36c-3b0a5f268ae1" :question/problem "Consider the set $B=(-1,\infty ).$ Complete the following reasoning to determine $inf(B)$ and $sup(B).$

The infimum of $B$ is the {{field-1}} of $B,$ and the supremum is the {{field-2}} of $B.$

Since $B$ is {{field-3}}, we have $inf(B)$ {{field-4}}.

Since $B$ is {{field-5}}, we have $sup(B)$ {{field-6}}."] ["question-60981b2b-035b-5158-a36c-3b0a5f268ae1" :question/worked-solution "The infimum of $B$ is the greatest lower bound of $B,$ and the supremum is the smallest upper bound of $B.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\le -1$ is smaller than or equal to the elements of $B.$ Thus, the set $(-\infty ,-1]$ contains only lower bounds of $B.$

- Any number in the set $x>-1$ is **not** a lower bound of $B.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $B$ that is smaller than $x$ for any $x>-1.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,-1]$ is the set of lower bounds of $B,$ and

$$
inf(B)=max(-\infty ,-1]=-1.
$$

Next, to find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

Since $B$ is unbounded above, $B$ has no upper bounds, and $sup(B)=+\infty .$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The infimum of a set $B$ is the $\text{greatest lower bound}$ of $B,$ and the supremum is the $\text{smallest upper bound}$ of $B.$

Since $B$ is $\text{bounded below},$ we have $inf(B)=-1.$

Since $B$ is $\text{unbounded above},$ we have $sup(B)=+\infty .$"] ["question-60981b2b-035b-5158-a36c-3b0a5f268ae1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] Therefore, {{field-4}}."] ["question-be9aa3b1-68a0-5981-aa70-f10a99f6fbac" :question/worked-solution "The supremum of a set $C$ is the smallest upper bound of $C.$

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $C$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\ge -1$ is greater than or equal to the elements of $C.$ Thus, the set $[-1,\infty )$ contains only upper bounds of $C.$

- Any number in the set $x<-1$ is **not** an upper bound of $C.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $C$ that is greater than $x$ for any $x<-1.$

Therefore, $[-1,\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $C,$ and

$$
sup(C)=min[-1,\infty )=-1.
$$

Notice that $-1$ is also the maximum of $C.$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The supremum of $C$ is the $\text{smallest upper bound}$ of $C.$

The set of upper bounds of $C$ is as follows:

$$
\{x\in R\,:\,x\ge -1\}
$$

Therefore, $sup(C)=-1\in C.$"] ["question-be9aa3b1-68a0-5981-aa70-f10a99f6fbac" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-cccdc7ac-4c98-5946-bd46-0e11422f5ea2" :answer-field/id :question/problem "Consider the set $B=(-\infty ,\pi \,].$ Complete the following reasoning to determine $inf(B)$ and $sup(B).$

The infimum of $B$ is the {{field-1}} of $B,$ and the supremum is the {{field-2}} of $B.$

Since $B$ is {{field-3}}, we have $inf(B)$ {{field-4}}.

Since $B$ is {{field-5}}, we have $sup(B)$ {{field-6}}."] ["question-f25266f1-2830-5a2e-9d12-da4f0e084a1d" :question/worked-solution "The infimum of $B$ is the greatest lower bound of $B,$ and the supremum is the smallest upper bound of $B.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

Since $B$ is unbounded below, $B$ has no lower bounds, and $inf(B)=-\infty .$

Next, to find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\ge \pi $ is greater than or equal to the elements of $B.$ Thus, the set $[\pi ,\infty )$ contains only upper bounds of $B.$

- Any number in the set $x<\pi $ is **not** an upper bound of $B.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $B$ that is greater than $x$ for any $x<\pi .$

Therefore, $[\pi ,\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $B,$ and

$$
sup(B)=min\,[\pi ,\infty )=\pi .
$$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The infimum of a set $B$ is the $\text{greatest lower bound}$ of $B,$ and the supremum is the $\text{smallest upper bound}$ of $B.$

Since $B$ is $\text{unbounded below},$ we have $inf(B)=-\infty .$

Since $B$ is $\text{bounded above},$ we have $sup(B)=\pi .$"] ["question-f25266f1-2830-5a2e-9d12-da4f0e084a1d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=-1+{(\frac{7}{10})}^{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/8b/8be6d8824c8cbf1fb66d64d3ccc027f2949149adc9f95cf4d1f3a814baec80b3.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing and converges to $-1.$ 

So, in our case, we have that

- any number in the set $x\le -1$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number in the set $x>-1$ is **not** a lower bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find a sufficiently large $n$ so that $-1+{(\frac{7}{10})}^{n}$ is smaller than $x$ for any $x>-1.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,-1]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
inf(A)=max(-\infty ,-1]=-1.
$$

Notice that $-1$ is *not* the minimum of $A$ (the set $A$ has no minimum). Therefore, we conclude that

$$
inf(A)=-1\notin A.

For this set, we have that {{field-1}}."] ["question-aafdf357-e5ff-5cb5-9dea-31946c44ff01" :question/worked-solution "The infimum of $A$ is the greatest lower bound of $A.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/42/42f6ea3d1c14b0ccb8774e284dc6812486ace7eda512e9c1b94df27e09445e6e.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is an oscillating sequence converging to $0.$ The minimum of $A$ is 

$$
min(A)={a}_{2}=\frac{(-1)^{2+1}}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $x\le {a}_{2}$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number $x>{a}_{2}$ cannot be a lower bound because ${a}_{2},$ an element of $A,$ is smaller than $x.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,-\frac{1}{2}]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
inf(A)=max(-\infty ,-\frac{1}{2}]=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Notice that $-\frac{1}{2}$ is the minimum of $A.$ Therefore, we conclude that

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=3-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/35/351e7bb3db6811be2a690fbd3fc2dc99282c4ff676e9116717d85515a298cf80.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is increasing and converges to $3.$ The minimum of $A$ is 

$$
min(A)={a}_{1}=3-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{1}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $x\le {a}_{1}$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number $x>{a}_{1}$ cannot be a lower bound because ${a}_{1},$ an element of $A,$ is smaller than $x.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,\frac{5}{2}]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
inf(A)=max(-\infty ,\frac{5}{2}]=\frac{5}{2}
$$

Notice that $\frac{5}{2}$ is the minimum of $A.$ Therefore, we conclude that

$$
inf(A)=\frac{5}{2}\in A.
$$"] ["question-13b42a92-bc61-5733-b661-85ce69e84b97" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-0d4e4ded-e058-51a6-b1cd-e47d3c47538e" :answer-field/id #uuid To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=2+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/78/7879f99e6dd09e7ada4c1d920b78504df70bf0c511380ea21728a755d6590d23.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing and converges to $2.$ 

So, in our case, we have that

- any number in the set $x\le 2$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number in the set $x>2$ is **not** a lower bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find a sufficiently large $n$ so that $2+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}$ is smaller than $x$ for any $x>2.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,2]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
inf(A)=max(-\infty ,2]=2.
$$

Notice that $2$ is *not* the minimum of $A$ (the set $A$ has no minimum). Therefore, we conclude that

$$

:knowledge-point/questions "question-5b171f8f-d26a-5943-99d9-8e4c4110d0e4"] [17592186163369 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn about the **supremum** of a set.

To get started, we first need to understand a related concept: the **upper bounds** of a set.

Given a set $A,$ a number $x$ is called an upper bound for $A$ if every element of $A$ is smaller than or equal to $x.$ 
Alternatively, $x$ is greater than or equal to every element of $A.$

For example, consider $A = \{1,2,3\}\subseteq \mathbb R.$ In this case, any number $x\geq 3$ is an upper bound of $A,$ since it is greater than or equal to $1, 2,$ and $3.$
So, $[3, \infty)$ is the set of upper bounds of $A.$

We will denote the set of the upper bounds of $A$ as $U_A.$

We can now proceed with the definition of **supremum**.

For a set $A$ that is bounded above, the supremum of $A$ is the minimum of $U_A.$ It is also called the **least upper bound** of $A.$

In our example $A = \{1,2,3\},$ we have

$$
\min(U_A) = \min [3, \infty) = 3.
$$

Thus, $\sup(A) = 3.$

Notice that, when a set has a maximum, the supremum equals the maximum. This holds, in particular, for non-empty finite sets.

This leads to the following result:

For any non-empty finite set, $\max(A) = \sup(A)$"] [17592186163203 :tutorial/content "Just as we defined the supremum, we now introduce the **infimum** of a set.

As we did for the supremum, we first need to define the lower bounds of a set.

Given a set $A,$ a number $x$ is called a **lower bound** for $A$ if every element of $A$ is greater than or equal to $x,$ or, alternatively, if $x$ is less than or equal to every element of $A.$

For example, for $A=\{1,2,3\}\subseteq \mathbb R,$ any number $x \leq 1$ is less than $1,$ $2,$ and $3.$ Therefore, $(-\infty, 1]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A.$

We will denote the set of the lower bounds of $A$ as $L_A.$

The infimum of a set $A$ is the maximum of $L_A,$ or the greatest lower bound of $A.$ 

For our set $A = \{1,2,3\},$ we have

$$
\max(L_A) = \max (-\infty, 1] = 1.
$$

Thus, $\inf(A) = 1.$

Again, we notice that the minimum of a set (provided that it exists) equals the infimum. As finite sets always have a minimum, this holds in particular for finite sets:

For any finite set, $\min(A) = \inf(A)$"] [17592186163200 :tutorial/content "Let's explore the supremum and infimum of intervals, starting with a closed interval.

**Example A:** $A = [0, 1].$

**Observation (Min/Max):**
Recall that if a set has a minimum and maximum, they correspond to the infimum and supremum.
Since $0$ and $1$ are bounds contained in $A,$ we have $\min(A)=0$ and $\max(A)=1.$ Thus, we expect:

$$
\inf (A) = 0, \qquad \sup (A) = 1.
$$

**Derivation using Sets of Bounds:**
To deepen our understanding, we verify this by finding the sets of lower and upper bounds ($L_A$ and $U_A$).

1\. **Infimum:** We identify $L_A$ and find its maximum.

  - Any number $x \leq 0$ is a lower bound for $A.$

  - Any number $x > 0$ is *not* a lower bound. Since $0 \in A$ and $0 < x,$ the number $x$ fails to be a lower bound.

  Therefore, $L_A = (-\infty, 0]$ and $\inf (A) = \max (-\infty, 0] = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}.$

2\. **Supremum:** We identify $U_A$ and find its minimum.

  - Any number $x \geq 1$ is an upper bound for $A.$

  - Any number $x < 1$ is *not* an upper bound. Since $1 \in A$ and $1 > x,$ the number $x$ fails to be an upper bound.

  Therefore, $U_A = [1, \infty)$ and $\sup (A) = \min [1, \infty) = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$"] [17592186163210 :tutorial/content "We now consider intervals where the endpoints are not necessarily included.

**Example B:** $B = (0, 1).$ 
The endpoints $0$ and $1$ are not in $B,$ so the set has **neither a maximum nor a minimum.**

However, the logical boundaries of the set remain the same.

- The set of lower bounds is $L_B = (-\infty, 0].$

$$
\inf (B) = \max (-\infty, 0] = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}.
$$

- The set of upper bounds is $U_B = [1, \infty).$

$$
\sup (B) = \min [1, \infty) = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.
$$"] [17592186163211 :tutorial/content "We continue by considering a half-open interval.

**Example C:** $C = [0, 1).$
Here, the inclusion is mixed.

- **Lower Bound:** $L_C = (-\infty, 0].$ 

$$
\inf (C) = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}
$$

Since $0 \in C,$ it is also the **minimum.**

- **Upper Bound:** $U_C = [1, \infty).$ 

$$
\sup (C) = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}
$$

Since $1 \notin C,$ the set has **no maximum.**"] [17592186163209 :tutorial/content "So far, we have dealt with bounded sets: sets that have both upper and lower bounds. Now, we consider unbounded sets.

If a set $A$ is unbounded above, then it has no upper bounds. In this case, we write

$$
\sup(A) = +\infty.
$$

Similarly, if a set $A$ is unbounded below, then it has no lower bounds. In this case, we write

$$
\inf(A) = -\infty.
$$

For example, consider the set $A = (1, \infty).$ This set is unbounded above, so $\sup(A) = +\infty.$ However, $A$ is bounded below, and $\inf(A) = 1.$"] [17592186163201 :tutorial/content "Consider the following set.

$$
A = \left\{ \left(\dfrac 12\right)^n \: : \: n\in \mathbb N \right\}
$$

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence $a_n,$ given by

$$
a_n =\left(\dfrac 12\right)^n, \qquad n \in \mathbb N = \{1,2,3,4,\ldots\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/b2/b2fc98fed45efbeb0ba7a1bfefe61d2f5698ab36b6c026bf5590b63d2da0a38a.png)

Notice that $a_n$ is a decreasing sequence. Therefore, the first term $a_1$ is the maximum of the set. Since $A$ has a maximum, the supremum equals the maximum:

$$
\sup(A) = \max(A) = a_1 = \dfrac 12
$$

Now, our set doesn't have a minimum: the points of the sequence get closer and closer to $0$ without reaching it. Let's find the infimum by determining the set of the lower bounds.

Notice that:

- any number $x \leq 0$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number $x > 0$ is **not** a lower bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find a sufficiently large $n$ so that $\left(\dfrac 12\right)^n$ is smaller than $x$ for any $x > 0.$

Therefore, $(-\infty, 0]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
\inf(A) = \max \big({-\infty}, 0\big] = 0.
$$"] [17592186163202 :tutorial/content "The concepts of supremum and infimum can be extended to functions.

Given a function $y=f(x),$ the **supremum** and the **infimum** of $f$ are, respectively, the supremum and the infimum of the range of $f.$

The **supremum** and **infimum** of a function will be denoted as

$$
\inf_{x\in D} f(x), \qquad \text{and} \sup_{x\in D} f(x),
$$

where $D$ is the domain of the function.

For example, consider the following parabola:

![](images/69/690b179ad127181eeb316fb9ae9c8085fa6aa96c6d4729c88d176a908950e80e.png)

The range of $f$ is $A = (-\infty, 0].$

Let's find the infimum and the supremum of $A.$

To find the infimum, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

In our case, $A$ has no lower bounds. For any real number $y,$ we can find an element $x$ such that $f(x) < y.$

Therefore, $\inf_{x\in \mathbb R} f(x) = -\infty.$

Next, to find the supremum, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $y \geq 0$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number $y < 0$ cannot be an upper bound of $A$ because $0,$ an element of $A,$ is greater than $y.$

Therefore, $[0,\infty)$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\sup_{x\in \mathbb R} f(x) = \sup(A) =\min[0,\infty)= 0.}
$$"] [17592186163370 :tutorial/content "**Theorem.** Suppose $A\subseteq \mathbb R$ is a non-empty set and $s$ is an upper bound of $A.$ Then $s = \sup A$ if and only if for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $a\in A$ such that

$$
s - \varepsilon < a.
$$

- **First, we prove that if $s = \sup A$ then for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $a\in A$ such that $s - \varepsilon < a.$**

By contradiction, suppose that there exists some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that there does not exist any $a\in A$ with $s - \varepsilon < a.$ Then, every element of $A$ is less than or equal to $s - \varepsilon.$ This implies that $s - \varepsilon$ is an upper bound of $A.$

Since $s$ is the least upper bound, we must have $s \le s - \varepsilon.$ However, since $\varepsilon > 0,$ we know that $s - \varepsilon < s.$ This is a contradiction.

- **Next, we prove that if for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $a\in A$ such that $s - \varepsilon < a,$ then $s = \sup A.$**

Again, by contradiction, assume $s \neq \sup A.$ Since $s$ is an upper bound of $A,$ the least upper bound must be strictly smaller than $s.$ Let $s_1 = \sup A,$ so $s_1 < s.$ 

Let $\varepsilon_1 = s - s_1.$ Since $s_1 < s,$ we have $\varepsilon_1 > 0.$
We can apply the property stated in the hypothesis to our $\varepsilon_1.$ So, there exists $a_1 \in A$ such that

$$
s - \varepsilon_1 < a_1.
$$

Substituting $\varepsilon_1 = s - s_1,$ we get $s - (s - s_1) < a_1,$ which simplifies to

$$
s_1 < a_1.
$$

Since $s_1$ is an upper bound of $A,$ we must have $a_1 \le s_1.$ This contradicts $s_1 < a_1.$ Thus, $s = \sup A.$"] [17592186163204 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we defined the infimum of a set as the maximum of the set of lower bounds, and the supremum as the minimum of the set of upper bounds.

If a set of real numbers is bounded and not empty, then the infimum exists and is a real number, and the supremum exists and is a real number.

This follows from the so-called **axiom of completeness**, a fundamental property of the real numbers that ensures that the real number line has no "gaps."

There are number sets, such as the set of rational numbers, that don't have this property. Consider for example the following subset of $\mathbb Q{:}$

$$
A = \{ q \in \mathbb Q \, : \, 1 < q^2 < 2 \}

Round your answer to the nearest integer."] ["question-533feaf7-7a54-5e3c-8829-f3324ed43a28" :question/worked-solution "We're told that the temperature of the exhaust pipe of a motorcycle is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-74).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-74} & =-0.08\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-74} & =-\int 0.08\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-74| & =-0.08t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-74>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-74 & ={e}^{-0.08t+C} \\ T-74 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T-74 & =K{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T & =74+K{e}^{-0.08t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was ${140}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=140,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}140 & =74+K{e}^{0} \\ 140 & =74+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=74+66{e}^{-0.08t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after $t=3$ minutes is

$$
T(3)=74+66{e}^{-0.08\cdot 3}≈{126}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

["question-1397b57e-0338-5e52-920b-2086a4adac56" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),\,Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\sqrt{\pi }
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
Γ(\frac{3}{2})=\frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi },
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(\frac{5}{2})=\frac{3}{2}Γ(\frac{3}{2})=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi }=\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
2\,Γ(\frac{5}{2})+Γ(\frac{3}{2})=2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi }=2\sqrt{\pi }.
$$"] ["question-1397b57e-0338-5e52-920b-2086a4adac56" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-68ee2d15-0779-5b6d-a0a3-58d2b6c1ee1b" :answer-field/id #uuid yards."] ["question-c5c07663-c2ba-5968-924a-8ce6b0b341c8" :question/worked-solution "The width of the plot is $x+5$ yards, and its area is $3{x}^{2}+15x$ square yards. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(3{x}^{2},15x)=3x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+15x & = \\ (3x\cdot x)+(3x\cdot 5)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x\cdot x)+(3x\cdot 5) & = \\ 3x(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $3x$ yards.

First, we write the expression as a difference of squares:

$$
{x}^{2}-25={x}^{2}-{5}^{2}
$$

Then, we factor the expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
{x}^{2}-25=(x+5)(x-5)
$$

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-8).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-8) \\ (-1) & \times 8 \\ 2 & \times (-4) \\ (-2) & \times 4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-8) & =-7 & \times  \\ -1+8 & =7 & \times  \\ 2+(-4) & =-2 & \times  \\ -2+4 & =2 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as $2x=4x-2x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-8 & ={x}^{2}+4x-2x-8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x-2x-8 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+4x)+(-2x-8) & = \\ x(x+4)-2(x+4) & = \\ (x-2)(x+4)\end{aligned}

 thousand dollars."] ["question-5c2f07e7-1da9-5f1b-b117-db8d520999a1" :question/worked-solution "The land initially costs $400$ thousand, which increases at a rate of $10%$ per year.

$10%$ as a decimal is $0.1.$ Therefore, an increase of $10%$ corresponds to multiplication by a factor of

$$
1+0.1=1.1.
$$

Therefore, we have:

* After $1$ year, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)$ thousand dollars

* After $2$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{2}$ thousand dollars

* After $3$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{3}$ thousand dollars

* After $4$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{4}$ thousand dollars

* After $5$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{5}$ thousand dollars 

Evaluating the expression for the value after $5$ years, we get the following:

$$
400\cdot (1.1)^{5}=644.204≈644,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, after $5$ years, the land will be worth approximately $644$ thousand dollars."] ["question-5c2f07e7-1da9-5f1b-b117-db8d520999a1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e7cb5d96-36e5-5198-87e5-6213f99e66e0" :answer-field/id #uuid "e7cb5d96-36e5-5198-87e5-6213f99e66e0"] ["answer-9a8cfaa5-8866-5393-910a-300c18a0c36a" :answer/id #uuid "9a8cfaa5-8866-5393-910a-300c18a0c36a"] ["answer-9a8cfaa5-8866-5393-910a-300c18a0c36a" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-9a8cfaa5-8866-5393-910a-300c18a0c36a" :answer/value "644"] ["answer-field-e7cb5d96-36e5-5198-87e5-6213f99e66e0" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-e7cb5d96-36e5-5198-87e5-6213f99e66e0" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-e7cb5d96-36e5-5198-87e5-6213f99e66e0" :answer-field/correct "answer-9a8cfaa5-8866-5393-910a-300c18a0c36a"] ["answer-field-e7cb5d96-36e5-5198-87e5-6213f99e66e0" :answer-field/choices "answer-9a8cfaa5-8866-5393-910a-300c18a0c36a"] ["question-5c2f07e7-1da9-5f1b-b117-db8d520999a1" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-e7cb5d96-36e5-5198-87e5-6213f99e66e0"] [17592186110626 :knowledge-point/questions "question-5c2f07e7-1da9-5f1b-b117-db8d520999a1"] ["question-2064e26a-7656-5c06-9eb5-86690541ec19" :question/id #uuid "2064e26a-7656-5c06-9eb5-86690541ec19"] ["question-2064e26a-7656-5c06-9eb5-86690541ec19" :question/math-academy-id "q-133799"] ["question-2064e26a-7656-5c06-9eb5-86690541ec19" :question/problem "The value $V(t)$ of Paul's plot of land, in thousands of dollars, can be modeled by the function $V(t)=400\cdot (1.1)^{t},$ where $t$ is the time in years since he bought the land. throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$"] [17592186234379 :question/worked-solution "To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["answer-field-9c2d58ce-95e5-572a-9ac2-e040031c4dfc" :answer-field/id #uuid "9c2d58ce-95e5-572a-9ac2-e040031c4dfc"] ["answer-a8e519cc-a7bd-5d74-8524-f56366c5b993" :answer/id #uuid $$

$$

$$

Then, we solve the remaining equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$

$$

Since the opposite of dividing by $3$ is multiplying by $3$, we apply the multiplication principle and multiply both sides of the equation by $3$:

$$

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(3,-4).$ So we have

$$
x-3=p{t}^{2},\,y+4=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p(x-3) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+4=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+4=-\frac{3}{2}t.

:question/problem "Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y+2)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(x+5)?$"] ["question-da2c9d27-2db1-52e6-a2e3-b28e1798b755" :question/worked-solution "The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(-5,-2).$ So we have

$$
x+5=p{t}^{2},\,y+2=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =\frac{1}{2}(x+5) \\ 4p(x+5) & =\frac{1}{2}(x+5) \\ 4p & =\frac{1}{2} \\ p & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+5=(\frac{1}{8}){t}^{2},\,y+2=2(\frac{1}{8})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+5=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2},\,y+2=\frac{1}{4}t.
$$"] ["question-da2c9d27-2db1-52e6-a2e3-b28e1798b755" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d889d998-6d7a-58b2-a490-fd41b8228c67" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

{{field-2}}."] [17592186070024 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to solve equations that contain absolute value expressions.

For example, let's consider the following equation:

$$
\mid x+1 \mid = 4
$$

For this equation to be true, either the *positive or negative* of the expression inside the absolute value must equal the right-hand side. That is,

$$
x+1 = 4 \qquad\qquad \text{or} \qquad\qquad -(x+1)=4
$$

So, let's solve these two equations:

- First, we solve the equation $x+1 = 4{:}$
$x + 1|= 4; x + 1 - 1|= 4 - 1; x|= 3$

- Then, we solve the equation $-(x+1) = 4{:}$
$- (x + 1)|= 4; - x - 1|= 4; - x - 1 + 1|= 4 + 1; - x|= 5; x|=-5$

Therefore, the solutions to our original absolute value equation are

$$
x={\color{blue}3}
$$

and

$$
x={\color{red}{-5}}
$$"] [17592186070025 :tutorial/content "So, we've seen that the solutions to the equation

$$
\mid x+1 \mid = 4
$$

are

$$

$$

and

$$

$$

We can verify that these solutions are correct by substituting them back into the original equation and checking we get a true statement:

- Substituting $x={\color{blue}3}$ into our equation, we get
$\mid x + 1 \mid |= 4; \mid 3 + 1 \mid |= 4; \mid 4 \mid |= 4; 4|= 4.✓$
Therefore, $x={\color{blue}3}$ is indeed a solution to the absolute value equation.
- Substituting $x={\color{red}-5}$ into our equation, we get
$\mid x + 1 \mid |= 4; \mid - 5 + 1 \mid |= 4; \mid - 4 \mid |= 4; 4|= 4.✓$
Therefore, $x={\color{red}-5}$ is indeed a solution to the absolute value equation.

Therefore,

$$
x={\color{blue}3}
$$

and

$$

$$

are both solutions to our absolute value equation."] [17592186166697 :question/problem "The disjoint union $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup A_3$ of events $A_1,A_2,A_3$ covers the entire sample space. Compute $P(A_1 \mid B)$ given the following probabilities:

$P(B\begin{vmatrix}A_{1}) = 0.23, \\ P(B \mid A_{2}) = 0.26,\end{vmatrix}P(A_{2}) = 0.3; P(B \mid A_{3}) = 0.18, \mid P(A_{3}) = 0.4$"] [17592186166697 :question/worked-solution "If the disjoint union $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup \ldots \sqcup A_n$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

$$
P(A_k \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{P(B \mid A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(B \mid A_i)P(A_i)}
$$

where

$$
k=1,2,\ldots,n
$$

In our case, $n=3$, and $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup A_3$ covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

$$
P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) = 1
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(A_{1}) &= 1 - (P(A_{2}) + P(A_{3})) \\
&= 1 - (0.3 + 0.4) \\
&= 0.3
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(A_{1}\begin{vmatrix}B) &= (P(B \mid A_{1})P(A_{1}))/(∑_(i = 1)^(3)P(B \mid A_{i})P(A_{i})) \\ = (P(B \mid A_{1})P(A_{1}))/(P(B \mid A_{1})P(A_{1}) + P(B \mid A_{2})P(A_{2}) + P(B\end{vmatrix}A_{3})P(A_{3})) \\
&= ((0.23)(0.3))/((0.23)(0.3) + (0.26)(0.3) + (0.18)(0.4)) \\
&= \frac{0.069}{0.219} \\
&\approx 0.315
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186166482 :question/problem "A travel agency offers three itineraries, itinerary $1$, itinerary $2$, and $3$. For each itinerary, customers can choose to travel using their own car or the agency's bus.

- Itinerary $1$ is chosen by $25\%$ of the customers, and $60\%$ of those customers travel by bus.
- Itinerary $2$ is chosen by $30\%$ of the customers, and $30\%$ of those customers travel by bus.
- Itinerary $3$ is chosen by $45\%$ of the customers, and $20\%$ of those customers travel by bus.

If $65\%$ of all customers travel with children, and $40\%$ of customers with children choose the bus, what is the probability that a randomly chosen customer that chooses the bus travels with children? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places."] [17592186166482 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be the event that a customer travels with children, $B$ be the event that a customer takes the bus, and $I_1, I_2, I_3$ be the event that a customer chooses itinerary $1$, $2$, or $3$, respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:
$\begin{bmatrix}P(I_{1}) = 0.25 & P(B \mid I_{1}) = 0.6 \\ P(I_{2}) = 0.3 & P(B \mid I_{2}) = 0.3 \\ P(I_{3}) = 0.45 & P(B \mid I_{3}) = 0.2\end{bmatrix}$
The disjoint union $I_1 \sqcup I_2 \sqcup I_3$ covers the entire sample space, and we have
$P(I_1)+ P(I_2) + P(I_3) = 0.25+0.3+0.45 = 1$.

- Since $65\%$ of customers have children, we have
$P(C) = 0.65$.
- Since $40\%$ of customers with children choose the bus, we have
$P(B \mid C) = 0.4$.

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen customer that chooses the bus travels with children, which is represented as $P(C \mid B)$.

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

Bayes' theorem states that

$$
P(A_1 \mid B)=\dfrac{P(B \mid A_1)P(A_1)}{P(B)}
$$

Now, the law of total probability tells us that

$$
P(B)=P(B \mid A_1)P(A_1) + P(B \mid A_2)P(A_2) + P(B \mid A_3)P(A_3)
$$

Substituting this into Bayes' theorem, we get

$$
P(A_1 \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A_1) P(A_1)}{P(B \mid A_1)P(A_1) + P(B \mid A_2)P(A_2) + P(B \mid A_3)P(A_3)}

$$

$$

which is usually written more compactly as

$$
P(A_k \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^3 P(B \mid A_i)P(A_i)}
$$

$$

$$

To demonstrate, let's consider the following absolute value equation:

$$
2 \mid x-1 \mid + 4 = 8
$$

We aim to isolate the $\mid x-1 \mid$ term on the left-hand side.

We start by subtracting $4$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}2 & x - 1 & + 4 &= 8 \\ 2 & x - 1 & + 4 - 4|= 8 - 4 \\ 2 & x - 1 & |= 4\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 \mid x - 1 \mid &= 4 \\
\frac{2 \mid x - 1\begin{vmatrix}}{2} &= \frac{4}{2} \\ \frac{2 \mid x - 1\end{vmatrix}}{2}|= 2 \\
\mid x - 1 \mid &= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

And that's it! We've successfully isolated the absolute value expression in our equation.

Let's consider another example."] [17592186193944 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following absolute value equation:

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $E$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x \geq 8$ is greater than or equal to the elements of $E$. Thus, the set $[8, \infty)$ contains only upper bounds of $E$.

Determine $\sup(A)$. Also determine whether or not $\sup(A)$ is in the set $A$."] [17592186161743 :question/worked-solution "The supremum of a set $A$ is the smallest upper bound of $A$.

{{field-1}}"] [17592186160509 :answer-field/choices 17592186160512] [17592186160509 :answer-field/choices 17592186160513] [17592186160509 :answer-field/choices 17592186160514] [17592186160509 :answer-field/choices 17592186160510] [17592186163369 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn about the **supremum** of a set.

To get started, we first need to understand a related concept: the **upper bounds** of a set.

Given a set $A$, a number $x$ is called an upper bound for $A$ if every element of $A$ is smaller than or equal to $x$.
Alternatively, $x$ is greater than or equal to every element of $A$.

For example, consider

$$
A = \{1,2,3\}\subseteq \mathbb R
$$

In this case, any number

$$
x\geq 3
$$

is an upper bound of $A$, since it is greater than or equal to $1, 2$, and $3$.
So, $[3, \infty)$ is the set of upper bounds of $A$.

We will denote the set of the upper bounds of $A$ as $U_A$.

We can now proceed with the definition of **supremum**.

For a set $A$ that is bounded above, the supremum of $A$ is the minimum of $U_A$. It is also called the **least upper bound** of $A$.

In our example

$$
A = \{1,2,3\}
$$

we have

$$
\min(U_A) = \min [3, \infty) = 3
$$

Thus,

$$
\sup(A) = 3
$$

Notice that, when a set has a maximum, the supremum equals the maximum. This holds, in particular, for non-empty finite sets.

This leads to the following result:

> For any non-empty finite set, $\max(A) = \sup(A)$"] [17592186163203 :tutorial/content "Just as we defined the supremum, we now introduce the **infimum** of a set.

Given a set $A$, a number $x$ is called a **lower bound** for $A$ if every element of $A$ is greater than or equal to $x$, or, alternatively, if $x$ is less than or equal to every element of $A$.

For example, for

$$
A=\{1,2,3\}\subseteq \mathbb R
$$

any number

$$
x \leq 1
$$

is less than $1$, $2$, and $3$. Therefore, $(-\infty, 1]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A$.

We will denote the set of the lower bounds of $A$ as $L_A$.

The infimum of a set $A$ is the maximum of $L_A$, or the greatest lower bound of $A$.

For our set

$$

we have

$$

Again, we notice that the minimum of a set (provided that it exists) equals the infimum. As finite sets always have a minimum, this holds in particular for finite sets:

> For any finite set, $\min(A) = \inf(A)$"] [17592186163200 :tutorial/content "Let's explore the supremum and infimum of intervals, starting with a closed interval.

**Example A:** $A = [0, 1]$.

**Observation (Min/Max):**
Recall that if a set has a minimum and maximum, they correspond to the infimum and supremum.
Since $0$ and $1$ are bounds contained in $A$, we have $\min(A)=0$ and $\max(A)=1$. Thus, we expect:

$$
\inf (A) = 0, \qquad \sup (A) = 1
$$

**Derivation using Sets of Bounds:**
To deepen our understanding, we verify this by finding the sets of lower and upper bounds ($L_A$ and $U_A$).

1. **Infimum:** We identify $L_A$ and find its maximum.Any number $x \leq 0$ is a lower bound for $A$.Any number $x > 0$ is *not* a lower bound. 2. **Supremum:** We identify $U_A$ and find its minimum.Any number $x \geq 1$ is an upper bound for $A$.Any number $x < 1$ is *not* an upper bound. \inf(A) = \max \big({-\infty}, 0\big] = 0
$$"] [17592186163202 :tutorial/content "The concepts of supremum and infimum can be extended to functions.

Given a function $y=f(x)$, the **supremum** and the **infimum** of $f$ are, respectively, the supremum and the infimum of the range of $f$.

The **supremum** and **infimum** of a function will be denoted as
$\inf_{x\in D} f(x), \qquad \text{and} \sup_{x\in D} f(x)$,
where $D$ is the domain of the function.

For example, consider the following parabola:

![](images/69/690b179ad127181eeb316fb9ae9c8085fa6aa96c6d4729c88d176a908950e80e.png)

The range of $f$ is

$$
A = (-\infty, 0]
$$

Let's find the infimum and the supremum of $A$.

To find the infimum, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

In our case, $A$ has no lower bounds. For any real number $y$, we can find an element $x$ such that $f(x) < y$.

Therefore,

$$
\inf_{x\in \mathbb R} f(x) = -\infty
$$

Next, to find the supremum, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $y \geq 0$ is an upper bound of $A$,
- any number $y < 0$ cannot be an upper bound of $A$ because $0$, an element of $A$, is greater than $y$.

Therefore, $[0,\infty)$ is the set of upper bounds of $A$, and

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\sup_{x\in \mathbb R} f(x) = \sup(A) =\min[0,\infty)= 0.}
$$"] [17592186163370 :tutorial/content "**Theorem.** Suppose $A\subseteq \mathbb R$ is a non-empty set and $s$ is an upper bound of $A$. Then $s = \sup A$ if and only if for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $a\in A$ such that
$s - \varepsilon < a$.

- **First, we prove that if $s = \sup A$ then for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $a\in A$ such that $s - \varepsilon < a$.**By contradiction, suppose that there exists some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that there does not exist any $a\in A$ with $s - \varepsilon < a$. Then, every element of $A$ is less than or equal to $s - \varepsilon$. This implies that $s - \varepsilon$ is an upper bound of $A$.Since $s$ is the least upper bound, we must have $s \le s - \varepsilon$. However, since $\varepsilon > 0$, we know that $s - \varepsilon < s$. This is a contradiction.
- **Next, we prove that if for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $a\in A$ such that $s - \varepsilon < a$, then $s = \sup A$.**Again, by contradiction, assume $s \neq \sup A$. Since $s$ is an upper bound of $A$, the least upper bound must be strictly smaller than $s$. Let $s_1 = \sup A$, so $s_1 < s$. Let $\varepsilon_1 = s - s_1$. Since $s_1 < s$, we have $\varepsilon_1 > 0$.
We can apply the property stated in the hypothesis to our $\varepsilon_1$. So, there exists $a_1 \in A$ such that
$s - \varepsilon_1 < a_1$.
Substituting $\varepsilon_1 = s - s_1$, we get $s - (s - s_1) < a_1$, which simplifies to
$s_1 < a_1$.
Since $s_1$ is an upper bound of $A$, we must have $a_1 \le s_1$. This contradicts $s_1 < a_1$. Thus, $s = \sup A$."] [17592186163204 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we defined the infimum of a set as the maximum of the set of lower bounds, and the supremum as the minimum of the set of upper bounds.

If a set of real numbers is bounded and not empty, then the infimum exists and is a real number, and the supremum exists and is a real number.

This follows from the so-called **axiom of completeness**, a fundamental property of the real numbers that ensures that the real number line has no "gaps."

There are number sets, such as the set of rational numbers, that don't have this property. Consider for example the following subset of $\mathbb Q{:}$

$$
A = \{q \in \mathbb Q \,: \, 1 < q^2 < 2 \}
$$

Notice that the rational numbers greater than $\sqrt 2$ are the upper bounds of $A$. However, this set has no minimum *in $\mathbb{Q}$*, so $\sup(A)$ doesn't exist."] [17592186172230 :question/problem "Evaluate $Γ(5)$."] [17592186064883 :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x) = 4x - \sin x$ and the point $P(0, 0)$ that lies on $y = f(x)$. Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P$, calculate $(f^{-1})^{′}(0)$."] [17592186234376 :question/problem "The following table gives the values of functions $f(x)$ and ${f}^{'}(x)$ at some points. Find $({f}^{-1})^{'}(5).$

| **$x$** | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{'}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $4$ | $9$ |
| $5$ | $1$ | $6$ |
| $8$ | $5$ | $4$ |"] [17592186234376 :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=5,$ we have

$$
({f}^{-1})^{'}(5)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(5))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${f}^{-1}(5)=8$ and ${f}^{'}(8)=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{'}(5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(8)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186234379 :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+1}{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2).$"] [17592186234379 :question/worked-solution "To determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{'}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{'}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186078164 :question/problem "Solve the equation $13 = \dfrac{6y+8}{2}$."] [17592186078164 :question/worked-solution "First, we clear the rational expression by multiplying both sides by $2$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 13 &= \dfrac{6y+8}{2} \\ 2 \cdot 13 &= 2 \cdot \left(\dfrac{6y+8}{2}\right) \\ 2 \cdot 13 &= \cancel{2} \cdot \left(\dfrac{6y+8}{\cancel{2}}\right) \\ 26 &= 6y+8 \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve the remaining equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned} 26 &= 6y+8 \\ 26-8 &= 6y+8-8 \\ 18 &= 6y \ \dfrac{18}{6} &= \dfrac{6y}{6} \\ 3 &= y \end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $y=3$."] [17592186078165 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac{a+2}{3} =a$."] [17592186078165 :question/worked-solution "First, we clear the rational expression by multiplying both sides by $3$:

$$
\require{cancel} \begin{aligned} \dfrac{a+2}{3} &=a \\ 3 \cdot \left(\dfrac{a+2}{3} \right) &= 3 \cdot a \ \cancel{3} \cdot \left(\dfrac{a+2}{\cancel{3}} \right) &= 3a \\ a+2 &= 3a \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve the remaining equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\require{cancel} \begin{aligned} a+2 &= 3a \\ a + 2 - a &= 3a - a \\ 2 &= 2a \ \dfrac{2}{2} &= \dfrac{2a}{2} \\ 1 &= a \end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $a=1$."] [17592186078166 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac{2n+6}{3} = 4n+1$."] [17592186078166 :question/worked-solution "First, we clear the rational expression by multiplying both sides by $3$. We must make sure that *all* of the terms on the right-hand side are multiplied by $3$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2n + 6}{3} &= 4n + 1 \\
3 \cdot (\frac{2n + 6}{3}) &= 3 \cdot (4n + 1) \\
3 \cdot (\frac{2n + 6}{3}) &= 3 \cdot 4n + 3 \cdot 1 \\
2n + 6 &= 12n + 3
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve the remaining equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2n + 6 &= 12n + 3 \\
2n + 6 - 2n &= 12n + 3 - 2n \\
6 &= 10n + 3 \\
6 - 3 &= 10n + 3 - 3 \\
3 &= 10n \\
\frac{3}{10} &= \frac{10n}{10} \\
\frac{3}{10} &= n
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
n = \dfrac{3}{10}
$$"] [17592186078167 :question/problem "Solve $\dfrac{5p+10}{6} =2(p-5)$."] [17592186078167 :question/worked-solution "First, we clear the rational expression by multiplying both sides by $6$:

$$
\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5p+10}{6} &=2(p-5) \\ 6 \cdot \left(\dfrac{5p+10}{6}\right) &=6\cdot 2 (p-5) \ \cancel{6} \cdot \left(\dfrac{5p+10}{\cancel{6}}\right) &=12(p-5) \\ 5p+10 &=12p-60 \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve the remaining equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned} 5p+10 &=12p-60 \\ 5p+10-5p &=12p-60-5p \\ 10 &=7p-60 \\ 10+60 &=7p-60+60 \\ 70 &=7p \ \dfrac{70}{7} &=\dfrac{7p}{7} \\ 10 &= p \end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $p=10$."] [17592186079717 :tutorial/content "Whenever we have a fraction in an equation, we apply the multiplication principle to get rid of it. For example, consider the equation below:

$$
\dfrac{2x+12}{3} =6
$$

Since the opposite of dividing by $3$ is multiplying by $3$, we apply the multiplication principle and multiply both sides of the equation by $3$:

$$
\require{cancel} \begin{aligned} \dfrac{2x+12}{3} &=6 \\ 3 \cdot \left(\dfrac{2x+12}{3}\right) &= 3 \cdot 6\ \cancel{3} \cdot \left(\dfrac{2x+12}{\cancel{3}}\right) &= 18 \\ 2x+12 &= 18 \end{aligned}
$$

The process of removing the fraction is called **clearing the rational expression**. We now have an equation that we can solve using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2x+12 &= 18 \\ 2x+12-12 &=18-12 \\ 2x &=6 \ \dfrac{2x}{2} &=\dfrac{6}{2} \\ x &=3 \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186157107 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-4,5),$ and passes through the point $(-2,3).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x - h = 2pt, \qquad y - k = pt^2,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-4,5),$ and so we have

$$
x + 4 = 2pt, \qquad y - 5 = pt^2.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-2, 3),$ we can substitute $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x + 4 = 2\left(-\dfrac12\right)t, \qquad y - 5 = \left(-\dfrac12\right)t^2 ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x + 4 = -t, \qquad y - 5 = -\dfrac12t^2 .
$$"] [17592186157108 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(-3,2),$ and passes through the point $(1,0).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-3,2),$ and so we have

$$

Since the parabola passes through $(1,0),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=0$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}4=p{t}^{2} \\ -2=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(-\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t^2, \qquad y -2 = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+3 = \dfrac{1}{4}t^2, \qquad y -2= \dfrac{1}{2}t .
$$"] [17592186157842 :question/problem "Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t ∈ (- ∞, ∞)$, generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(1,-2)$ and which passes through the point $(-3, 6)$?"] [17592186155973 :answer-field/choices 17592186155974] [17592186155973 :answer-field/choices 17592186155975] [17592186155973 :answer-field/choices 17592186155976] [17592186155973 :answer-field/choices 17592186155977] [17592186155973 :answer-field/choices 17592186155978] [17592186354344 :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(2,-2),$ and passes through the point $(4,2).$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=3{t}^{2},\,y+1=6t.
$$"] [17592186175761 :question/problem "From the information given below, find all of the angles that are congruent.
$m∠A|= 10^{∘},; m∠B|= 40^{∘},; m∠C|= 80^{∘},; m∠D|= 90^{∘} - m∠C,; m∠E|= m∠B$."] [17592186175761 :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the measures of $\angle D$ and $\angle E$:

$$
\begin{aligned}

So, we have:

$$

and

- If $\left| \dfrac{7}{2}z-2 \right| = \dfrac{7}{2}z-2$, we obtain:
$\mid \frac{7}{2}z - 2 \mid |= 3; \frac{7}{2}z - 2|= 3; \frac{7}{2}z|= 5$

$\frac{7}{2}z|= 5; (\frac{2}{7}) \cdot (\frac{7}{2}z)|= (\frac{2}{7}) \cdot (5); (\frac{2}{7}) \cdot (\frac{7}{2}z)|= \frac{10}{7}; z|= \frac{10}{7}$.
- If $\left| \dfrac{7}{2}z-2 \right| = -\left(\dfrac{7}{2}z-2\right)$, we obtain:
$\mid \frac{7}{2}z - 2 \mid |= 3; - (\frac{7}{2}z - 2)|= 3; - \frac{7}{2}z + 2|= 3; - \frac{7}{2}z|= 1$
Multiplying both sides of the equation by $-\dfrac{2}{7}$ gives
$-\frac{7}{2}z|= 1; (-\frac{2}{7}) \cdot (-\frac{7}{2}z)|= (-\frac{2}{7}) \cdot (1); (-\frac{2}{7}) \cdot (-\frac{7}{2}z)|=-\frac{2}{7}; z|=-\frac{2}{7}$.

Therefore, the solutions are

$$
z = -\dfrac{2}{7}
$$

and

$$
z = \dfrac{10}{7}

For example, let's consider the following equation:

$$
\mid x+1 \mid = 4
$$

For this equation to be true, either the *positive or negative* of the expression inside the absolute value must equal the right-hand side. That is,

$$
x+1 = 4 \qquad\qquad \text{or} \qquad\qquad -(x+1)=4
$$

So, let's solve these two equations:

- First, we solve the equation $x+1 = 4{:}$
$x + 1|= 4; x + 1 - 1|= 4 - 1; x|= 3$

- Then, we solve the equation $-(x+1) = 4{:}$
$- (x + 1)|= 4; - x - 1|= 4; - x - 1 + 1|= 4 + 1; - x|= 5; x|=-5$

Therefore, the solutions to our original absolute value equation are

$$
x={\color{blue}3}
$$

and

$$
x={\color{red}{-5}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35d16431-4611-59fc-8888-c1db1a7b9902" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8821 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0212403d-0f66-5be5-8ebb-0dcacbe7f08f" :step/math-academy-id 143132 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069593}} {:db/id 17592186069593 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070025 :tutorial/content "So, we've seen that the solutions to the equation

\mid x+1 \mid = 4
$$

are

$$
x={\color{blue}3}
$$

and

$$
x={\color{red}{-5}}
$$

We can verify that these solutions are correct by substituting them back into the original equation and checking we get a true statement:

- Substituting $x={\color{blue}3}$ into our equation, we get
$\mid x + 1 \mid |= 4; \mid 3 + 1 \mid |= 4; \mid 4 \mid |= 4; 4|= 4.✓$
Therefore, $x={\color{blue}3}$ is indeed a solution to the absolute value equation.
- Substituting $x={\color{red}-5}$ into our equation, we get
$\mid x + 1 \mid |= 4; \mid - 5 + 1 \mid |= 4; \mid - 4 \mid |= 4; 4|= 4.✓$
Therefore, $x={\color{red}-5}$ is indeed a solution to the absolute value equation.

Therefore,

$$
x={\color{blue}3}
$$

and

$$
x={\color{red}{-5}}
$$

are both solutions to our absolute value equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "561ffe88-9340-5e0a-840a-6946f446a9f2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8822 :tutorial/title "Checking the Solution"} :step/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186166697 :question/id #uuid "699d9c0c-bb98-5710-8d98-10b6f35ab202" :question/math-academy-id "e-8911" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166847 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e9d77603-c824-5160-80fc-3d10353fe243" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Conditional Probability Using Bayes' Theorem"}] :question/problem "The disjoint union $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup A_3$ of events $A_1,A_2,A_3$ covers the entire sample space. Compute $P(A_1 \mid B)$ given the following probabilities:

$P(B\begin{vmatrix}A_{1}) = 0.23, \\ P(B \mid A_{2}) = 0.26,\end{vmatrix}P(A_{2}) = 0.3; P(B \mid A_{3}) = 0.18, \mid P(A_{3}) = 0.4$" :question/worked-solution "If the disjoint union $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup \ldots \sqcup A_n$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

$$
P(A_k \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{P(B \mid A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(B \mid A_i)P(A_i)}
$$

where

$$
k=1,2,\ldots,n
$$

In our case, $n=3$, and $A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup A_3$ covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

$$
P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) = 1
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(A_{1}) &= 1 - (P(A_{2}) + P(A_{3})) \\
&= 1 - (0.3 + 0.4) \\
&= 0.3
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(A_{1}\begin{vmatrix}B) &= (P(B \mid A_{1})P(A_{1}))/(∑_(i = 1)^(3)P(B \mid A_{i})P(A_{i})) \\ = (P(B \mid A_{1})P(A_{1}))/(P(B \mid A_{1})P(A_{1}) + P(B \mid A_{2})P(A_{2}) + P(B\end{vmatrix}A_{3})P(A_{3})) \\
&= ((0.23)(0.3))/((0.23)(0.3) + (0.26)(0.3) + (0.18)(0.4)) \\
&= \frac{0.069}{0.219} \\
&\approx 0.315
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048412} {:db/id 17592186049605} {:db/id 17592186167115 :question/id #uuid "b7f933e2-5017-50df-b8ef-7fd429d6b6ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-147126" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166847 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e9d77603-c824-5160-80fc-3d10353fe243" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Conditional Probability Using Bayes' Theorem"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b8dac953-8c37-59e7-8fe0-02995240c8a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.367" :db/id 17592186163769} {:answer/id #uuid "e7a3e076-7caa-5547-9a00-710bdb26a958" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.275" :db/id 17592186163770} {:answer/id #uuid "0065bdc3-5a85-580a-b646-c0c3f8b3a082" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.427" :db/id 17592186163771} {:answer/id #uuid "378ab112-fb34-5f2f-a941-6b455f5fc293" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.435" :db/id 17592186163772} {:answer/id #uuid "4fa843b3-4375-5967-9938-b21632b67e71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.395" :db/id 17592186163773}] :answer-field/id #uuid "e72dc4b4-bf09-5d67-8671-75165506e5e6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186163768}] :question/problem "The disjoint union $A_{1}⊔A_{2}⊔A_{3}$ of events $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}$ covers the entire sample space. - $36\%$ of the potatoes are of variety $1$, and $20\%$ of those potatoes weigh more than $100\,\mathrm g$.
- $17\%$ of the potatoes are of variety $2$, and $6\%$ of those potatoes weigh more than $100\,\mathrm g$.
- $47\%$ of the potatoes are of the variety $3$.

If $16\%$ of potatoes from the entire farm are sold to a local restaurant, $40\%$ of potatoes sold to the restaurant weigh more than $100\,\mathrm g$, and $15\%$ of potatoes that weigh more than $100\,\mathrm g$ are sold to the restaurant, what is the probability that a randomly selected potato from variety $3$ weighs more than $100\,\mathrm g$? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $R$ be the event that a potato is sold to the restaurant, $W$ be the event that a potato weighs more than $100\,\mathrm g$, and $V_1, V_2, V_3$ be the event that a potato is of variety $1$, $2$, or $3$, respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:
$P(V_{1}) = 0.36\begin{vmatrix}P(W \mid V_{1}) = 0.2 \\ P(V_{2}) = 0.17\end{vmatrix}P(W \mid V_{2}) = 0.06; P(V_{3}) = 0.47$
The disjoint union $V_1 \sqcup V_2 \sqcup V_3$ covers the entire sample space, and we have
$P(V_1)+ P(V_2) + P(V_3) = 0.36+0.17+0.47 = 1$.
- Since $16\%$ of potatoes from the entire farm are sold to a local restaurant, we have
$P(R) = 0.16$.
- Since $40\%$ potatoes sold to the restaurant weigh more than $100\,\mathrm g$, we have
$P(W \mid R) = 0.4$.
- Since $15\%$ of potatoes that weigh more than $100\,\mathrm g$ are sold to the restaurant, we have
$P(R \mid W) = 0.15$.

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen potato of variety $3$ weighs more than $100\,\mathrm g$, which is represented as $P(W \mid V_3)$.

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(R\begin{vmatrix}W) &= (P(W \mid R)P(R))/(P(W)) \\ P(R \mid W)|= (P(W \mid R)P(R))/(P(W \mid V_{1})P(V_{1}) + P(W \mid V_{2})P(V_{2}) + P(W \mid V_{3})P(V_{3})) \\ 0.15|= ((0.4)(0.16))/((0.2)(0.36) + (0.06)(0.17) + P(W \mid V_{3})(0.47)) \\ 0.15|= (0.064)/(0.0822 + 0.47P(W\end{vmatrix}V_{3}))
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(W \mid V_3)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.15(0.0822 + 0.47P(W\begin{vmatrix}V_{3})) &= 0.064 \\ 0.0822 + 0.47P(W \mid V_{3})|= \frac{0.064}{0.15} \\ 0.0822 + 0.47P(W \mid V_{3})|= \frac{32}{75} \\ 0.47P(W \mid V_{3})|= \frac{32}{75} - 0.0822 \\ P(W \mid V_{3})|= \frac{1}{0.47}(\frac{32}{75} - 0.0822) \\ P(W \mid V_{3})\end{vmatrix}\approx 0.733
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186167117 :question/id #uuid "e39e7e2c-b39e-5302-b92e-8f13f6ffd98c" :question/math-academy-id "q-147235"} {:db/id 17592186167119 :question/id #uuid "5b92de6f-2dd5-5916-8078-94243b8290b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-148674"} {:db/id 17592186275200 :question/id #uuid "cbae7601-74f3-53d4-af26-b2c79a262289" :question/math-academy-id "q-148669"} {:db/id 17592186166877 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166482 :question/id #uuid "bc694d40-d150-55e6-981f-0ca6b5d91e21" :question/math-academy-id "e-10418"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6c467adb-9d0e-5b33-b81e-4959e2703535" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167052 :question/id #uuid "e6e6c65a-4f3f-5fa3-ad82-a3b49ed0dc13" :question/math-academy-id "q-104789"} {:db/id 17592186167118 :question/id #uuid "dea495bf-07d9-54cd-baea-bb953539d3dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-148673"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying Bayes’ Theorem to a Situation in Context"} {:db/id 17592186166482 :question/id #uuid "bc694d40-d150-55e6-981f-0ca6b5d91e21" :question/math-academy-id "e-10418" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166877 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6c467adb-9d0e-5b33-b81e-4959e2703535" :knowledge-point/title "Applying Bayes’ Theorem to a Situation in Context"}] :question/problem "A travel agency offers three itineraries, itinerary $1$, itinerary $2$, and $3$. For each itinerary, customers can choose to travel using their own car or the agency's bus.

- Itinerary $1$ is chosen by $25\%$ of the customers, and $60\%$ of those customers travel by bus.
- Itinerary $2$ is chosen by $30\%$ of the customers, and $30\%$ of those customers travel by bus.
- Itinerary $3$ is chosen by $45\%$ of the customers, and $20\%$ of those customers travel by bus.

If $65\%$ of all customers travel with children, and $40\%$ of customers with children choose the bus, what is the probability that a randomly chosen customer that chooses the bus travels with children? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be the event that a customer travels with children, $B$ be the event that a customer takes the bus, and $I_1, I_2, I_3$ be the event that a customer chooses itinerary $1$, $2$, or $3$, respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:
$\begin{bmatrix}P(I_{1}) = 0.25 & P(B \mid I_{1}) = 0.6 \\ P(I_{2}) = 0.3 & P(B \mid I_{2}) = 0.3 \\ P(I_{3}) = 0.45 & P(B \mid I_{3}) = 0.2\end{bmatrix}$
The disjoint union $I_1 \sqcup I_2 \sqcup I_3$ covers the entire sample space, and we have
$P(I_1)+ P(I_2) + P(I_3) = 0.25+0.3+0.45 = 1$.

- Since $65\%$ of customers have children, we have
$P(C) = 0.65$.
- Since $40\%$ of customers with children choose the bus, we have
$P(B \mid C) = 0.4$.

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen customer that chooses the bus travels with children, which is represented as $P(C \mid B)$.

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
